chapters.title: Chapter 2: The New Toolkit of Economic Statecraft

lessons.title: Tariffs, Sanctions and Export Controls as Strategic Weapons

children.text: On 28 February 2022, the Moscow Exchange simply stopped trading. Not because of a crash in the ordinary sense, but because Russian equities had become, almost overnight, a different kind of asset: one a Western investor could no longer legally sell. Compare that to a tariff announcement, which typically unfolds over weeks of leaks, negotiation and phased implementation. Both are tools of what analysts now call economic statecraft, using trade and financial policy to pursue strategic goals, but they behave completely differently in a portfolio. Confusing the two, treating a sanctions risk like a tariff risk, is one of the more expensive mistakes a macro investor can make in this environment.

body.text: Tariffs, sanctions and export controls are not three flavours of the same policy. They target different things, they escalate on different timelines, and they price into markets in fundamentally different ways. Treat them as one undifferentiated "geopolitical risk" and you will misjudge both the speed and the size of the market reaction.

children.text: A tariff is a tax on an import, paid by the importer, not the exporting country's government, and in practice passed through to consumer or business prices to varying degrees. It is a revenue and leverage tool: the country imposing it wants either money, or a change in the other side's behaviour, or both, and it can be dialled up or down in increments as negotiations evolve.

A sanction blocks a transaction, an asset or a counterparty outright, typically through the banking system. It is a denial tool: freezing a central bank's reserves, cutting banks off from SWIFT messaging, or barring a company from touching the dollar system are not taxes to be negotiated down, they are switches that are either on or off.

markDefs.definition: A US export control mechanism extending US jurisdiction to foreign-made products that were produced using US-origin technology, software or equipment above a specified threshold, allowing Washington to restrict sales it does not directly control, such as a Dutch or Taiwanese company's chip-related exports.

children.text: An export control restricts a specific good or technology from reaching a specific buyer, regardless of price or willingness to pay. It is a capability-denial tool, aimed at preventing a rival from acquiring something strategically useful, most visibly advanced semiconductors and the equipment used to make them. Because the goal is denial rather than revenue, export controls do not respond to economic pain the way tariffs sometimes do, and the
lets Washington extend this reach well beyond its own borders.

children.text: Case Study: US Export Controls on Advanced Semiconductors

On 7 October 2022, the US Bureau of Industry and Security imposed sweeping restrictions on exporting advanced AI and high-performance computing chips, and the equipment used to manufacture them, to China. The rules did not stop at chips designed in America. Through the Foreign Direct Product Rule, they also reached the Dutch company ASML, whose extreme ultraviolet lithography machines are the only tools in the world capable of printing the most advanced chip circuitry, and effectively barred ASML from selling its newest EUV machines to Chinese customers. Nvidia, whose most advanced AI chips were the direct target, had to design cut-down versions specifically to stay just under the new performance thresholds, only for Washington to tighten the rules again in October 2023 and close that gap.

children.text: Huawei is the sharpest illustration of how narrow and devastating an export control can be. Its global smartphone shipments, briefly the world's second largest behind Samsung in 2019, collapsed within two years once it lost access to Google's mobile services and to advanced chip fabrication, a decline no tariff of any size could have produced, because a tariff would only have made Huawei's phones more expensive, not impossible to build at the cutting edge.

body.label: Huawei global smartphone rank, 2019 to 2021
body.value: #2 worldwide to a fraction of that
body.context: Collapse driven by loss of Google Mobile Services and advanced chip fabrication access, not by any tariff.

children.text: Case Study: The Russia Sanctions Package

The response to Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine showed the full sanctions toolkit deployed at once: major Russian banks cut off from SWIFT messaging, roughly $300 billion of the Russian central bank's foreign reserves held abroad frozen, and, from December 2022, a G7 price cap of $60 a barrel on Russian seaborne crude, enforced by barring Western shipping and insurance services to cargoes sold above that level. Russian equities were removed from the MSCI Emerging Markets Index within weeks, effectively valued at zero for any index-tracking fund, regardless of what the companies themselves were still worth.

body.text: The price cap is a hybrid instrument worth noting on its own: it behaves partly like a sanction (enforced through binary access to shipping and insurance services) and partly like a negotiated ceiling (set at a level meant to keep Russian oil flowing to global markets, just at a discount). It is a reminder that these three tools increasingly get combined and customised rather than used in pure form.

children.text: India's Own Toolkit Is Smaller, and Used Differently

India does not run a global sanctions or export control regime comparable to Washington's, and generally does not participate in sanctions it has not separately agreed to through the UN Security Council, a stance it maintained visibly with Russia. Its own instruments sit mostly on the tariff side: anti-dumping and countervailing duties, administered through the Directorate General of Trade Remedies, are used routinely against underpriced imports, from Chinese steel to solar cells, and import restrictions are increasingly tied to domestic manufacturing incentives like the PLI schemes this course examines in Chapter 4. These are narrower tools than what the US or EU deploy, but they still move specific NSE and BSE-listed sectors sharply when announced, which is exactly why a macro investor tracking India needs to watch DGTR notifications the way a US-focused investor watches BIS Entity List updates.

body.title: Match the tool to the mechanism
body.question: A country wants to prevent a rival's technology sector from acquiring a specific class of advanced manufacturing equipment, regardless of the price the rival is willing to pay. Which tool fits this goal?
options: A financial sanction on the buyer's banks
An export control on the equipment itself
body.explanation: This is a capability-denial goal, not a revenue or price goal, which is exactly what export controls are built for. A tariff would only raise the price, not prevent acquisition, and a financial sanction targets the buyer's access to money rather than the specific good.

body.title: Assess a new export control announcement
body.scenario: You cover an Indian electronics contract manufacturer that assembles devices for global brands using a mix of components, some sourced from a country recently hit with new US chip export controls similar to the 2022 and 2023 rounds against China.
body.prompt: List the two or three specific questions you would need answered before deciding whether this new export control is a direct risk to your company's supply chain, versus a risk that applies mainly to its competitors or suppliers further upstream.
body.modelAnswer: Reasonable questions include: (1) Does the restricted category of chips or equipment actually appear in this company's bill of materials, or does it use lower-end components that fall outside the restricted performance thresholds? (2) Does the Foreign Direct Product Rule reach any of this company's own suppliers, even if they are not American or Chinese, because of US-origin tooling somewhere in their production process? (3) Is the company positioned as a beneficiary of the resulting rerouting, similar to the connector-country pattern from Chapter 1, gaining assembly business precisely because a competitor elsewhere lost access to a restricted input? An export control's impact is rarely uniform across an entire sector, it depends on exactly where a company sits in the restricted supply chain.

cards.definition: The use of trade, financial and investment policy tools, such as tariffs, sanctions and export controls, to pursue strategic and geopolitical goals rather than purely economic ones.
A US Commerce Department list of foreign companies and organisations subject to export restrictions, used against Huawei from May 2019 and against numerous Chinese chip-sector firms since.
A US export control mechanism reaching foreign-made products built using US-origin technology, software or equipment, allowing restrictions on non-US companies like ASML.
A hybrid sanctions tool, used on Russian seaborne crude from December 2022, that permits trade below a set price while cutting off shipping and insurance access above it.

points: Tariffs are revenue and leverage tools that escalate gradually and are usually negotiable, so markets price them in over weeks.
Sanctions are denial tools that block transactions or assets outright, and typically reprice markets suddenly and sharply, as the February 2022 MOEX trading halt showed.

Export controls deny access to a specific capability regardless of price, which is why they can devastate a single company, as Huawei's post-2019 collapse shows, without moving broader trade statistics much at all.
The Foreign Direct Product Rule lets Washington's export controls reach far beyond US borders, pulling in companies like ASML that are not American at all.
India relies mainly on tariff-side tools such as anti-dumping duties rather than sanctions or export controls, but these still move specific NSE and BSE-listed sectors sharply when announced.
Because these three tools behave so differently, the first question on any new policy headline should be which of the three it actually is, not just how large or aggressive it sounds.
